Browse All / Neuroblastoma

Neuroblastoma

MONDO:0005072 Pathograph 13 Show in embeddings browser neuroblastic tumor

Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood, arising from neural crest-derived sympathetic nervous system precursors. It demonstrates remarkable clinical heterogeneity, ranging from spontaneous regression in infants to highly aggressive metastatic disease in older children. MYCN amplification, present in approximately 20% of cases, is among the most powerful adverse genomic prognostic markers and drives aggressive tumor behavior. Risk stratification in the INRG system combines stage, age, histologic category and grade of differentiation, MYCN status, chromosome 11q status, and DNA ploidy to guide treatment intensity. A distinct axis of neuroblastoma biology is the mechanism of telomere maintenance: telomerase is activated through TERT rearrangement, MYCN amplification or high TERT expression without either alteration, while alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), often with ATRX alteration, maintains telomeres without telomerase. The two mechanisms are almost mutually exclusive. ATRX-altered disease is enriched in older children, adolescents and young adults and often runs a slow but progressive course, with poor response to induction chemotherapy reported for large ATRX deletions and truncating mutations. Low-risk neuroblastoma may require only observation, while high-risk disease requires intensive multimodal therapy with immunotherapy.

Mappings

MONDO
MONDO:0005072 neuroblastoma
skos:exactMatch MONDO
Primary MONDO identifier for this entry. MONDO defines the class as an extracranial childhood cancer that originates from neural crest tissues of the sympathetic nervous system, matching this entry's scope, and records NCIT:C3270 and Orphanet:635 as exact matches. MONDO also files olfactory, cerebral and retinal neuroblastoma, and adrenal gland and mediastinum ganglioneuroblastoma, beneath the class; this entry does not cover them (see notes).
NCIT
NCIT:C3270 Neuroblastoma
skos:exactMatch NCIT
NCIT concept that MONDO records as an exact match of MONDO:0005072. NCIT defines it as a malignant neuroblastic tumor with neuroblastic cells, no ganglion cells and no prominent Schwannian stroma, matching this entry. NCIT also files olfactory neuroblastoma (NCIT:C3789), CNS neuroblastoma with FOXR2 activation (NCIT:C186547) and retinal neuroblastoma (NCIT:C6956) beneath it; this entry does not cover them (see notes). NCIT also has a narrower Peripheral Neuroblastoma class (NCIT:C6591); C3270 is used because it is the class MONDO records as an exact match, and NCIT files this disease's stage, risk-group and differentiation-grade classes under C3270 rather than under C6591.

Subtypes

3
molecular
MYCN-Amplified Neuroblastoma
Approximately 20% of neuroblastomas harbor MYCN gene amplification, associated with rapid tumor progression and poor prognosis. MYCN amplification is one of the earliest oncogene amplifications discovered.
Show evidence (4 references)
PMID:41560679 SUPPORT BACKGROUND Human Clinical
"MYCN amplification is a key factor contributing to the poor prognosis of NB."
States the adverse prognostic association of MYCN amplification. The sentence is background in the abstract of an iPSC-derived neural crest model study, restating the clinical picture; it is not something that study measured. The patient-derived support is the Brodeur and INRG evidence below.
PMID:6719137 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Furthermore, N-myc amplification is highly correlated with advanced stages of disease (P less than 0.001) and with the ability to grow in vitro as an established cell line, both of which are associated with a poor prognosis."
Human clinical support for the rapid-progression and poor-prognosis claim, from untreated primary neuroblastoma tissue.
PMID:19047291 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Stage, age, histologic category, grade of tumor differentiation, the status of the MYCN oncogene, chromosome 11q status, and DNA ploidy were the most highly statistically significant and clinically relevant factors."
Confirms MYCN status as a statistically significant, clinically relevant prognostic factor in the 8,800-patient INRG cohort.

risk group
High-Risk Neuroblastoma NCIT:C150281
A pretreatment risk group that sets treatment intensity, not a histologic or molecular entity; which tumors it contains depends on the classification system. In the International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) classification (2009), which defines 16 pretreatment groups, high risk denotes the groups with 5-year event-free survival below 50%, and 18 months was selected as the age cutoff. The Children's Oncology Group (COG) classifier version 2 (2021) uses the INRG Staging System (INRGSS) and adds segmental chromosome aberrations. Among stage L1, L2 and M tumors, it classifies as high risk stage M at 18 months or older, MYCN-amplified stage M at any age and stage M in toddlers aged 12 to under 18 months with any unfavorable biomarker, as well as MYCN-amplified L2 tumors, L2 tumors without MYCN amplification but with unfavorable International Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification (INPC) histology at 18 months or older, and incompletely resected MYCN-amplified L1 tumors. Its rules for stage MS are set out separately; for stages M and MS together, MYCN status affected risk group assignment in children younger than 12 months, and MYCN status, histology, ploidy and segmental chromosome aberrations did so at 12 to 18 months. The International Society of Pediatric Oncology European Neuroblastoma Group (SIOPEN) high-risk trial HR-NBL1 took patients older than 12 months with International Neuroblastoma Staging System (INSS) stage 4 disease and patients with MYCN-amplified stage 2, 3 or 4 disease. In the SIOPEN HR-NBL1.5 study, random assignment between two induction regimens used a 1-year age threshold: it was open to patients aged 1 to 20 years with stage 4 disease and to infants younger than 1 year with MYCN-amplified stage 4 or 4S disease. High-risk treatment typically includes myeloablative therapy and immunotherapy.

PMID:19047291 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"The optimal age cutoff was determined to be between 15 and 19 months, and 18 months was selected for the classification system. Sixteen pretreatment groups were defined on the basis of clinical criteria and statistically significantly different EFS of the cohort stratified by the INRG criteria...."
The INRG Task Force report found the optimal age cutoff to lie between 15 and 19 months, and the Task Force selected 18 months for the classification system. The risk categories are survival bands from this pooled cohort.

High risk is one of the groups this classifier assigns; the paper notes that risk schemas differ across cooperative groups.

These are COG-specific rules.

anatomic
Adrenal Gland Neuroblastoma MONDO:0006076
Neuroblastoma whose primary tumor arises in the adrenal gland. In the INRG database, 47% of 8,369 children with neuroblastoma or ganglioneuroblastoma and a known primary site had adrenal tumors. After adjustment for age, stage and histologic grade, adrenal primaries had about twice the odds of MYCN amplification of non-adrenal primaries (adjusted odds ratio 2.09), and after adjustment for age, MYCN status and stage they carried a modestly higher risk of events (hazard ratio 1.13).
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:25154816 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Among 8,369 children, 47% had adrenal tumors. ... Adrenal tumors were more likely than nonadrenal tumors (adjusted odds ratio, 2.09; 95% CI, 1.67 to 2.63; P < .001) and thoracic tumors were less likely than nonthoracic tumors (adjusted odds ratio, 0.20; 95% CI, 0.11 to 0.39; P < .001) to have..."
In the INRG database cohort of children younger than 21 years diagnosed with neuroblastoma or ganglioneuroblastoma in 1990-2002 with a known primary site, 47% of the 8,369 children had adrenal primary tumors. Compared with non-adrenal primaries, adrenal tumors had about twice the odds of MYCN amplification after adjustment for age, stage and histologic grade (adjusted odds ratio 2.09), and a higher risk of an event after adjustment for age, MYCN status and stage (hazard ratio 1.13). Because the cohort includes ganglioneuroblastoma, the 47% is a share of this cohort, not a frequency among neuroblastoma alone.

Pathophysiology

Neural Crest Developmental Arrest
Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest-derived sympathoadrenal progenitor cells that fail to complete differentiation. The tumor cells retain characteristics of immature neuroblasts with variable capacity for sympathetic neuronal differentiation.

MYCN-Driven Proliferation
MYCN amplification results in massive overexpression of the MYCN transcription factor, a key contributor to aggressive neuroblastoma biology and poor prognosis. MYCN-amplified tumors have a distinct aggressive phenotype with rapid growth and early metastasis.

Xenopus anteroventral noradrenergic (AVNA) cell differentiation model Xenopus laevis perturbs Positions MYCN upstream of the differentiation block: MYCN overexpression prevents Ascl1-driven differentiation, and loses that ability when Ascl1 cannot be phosphorylated.
Downstream
Telomerase Activation Amplified MYCN raises TERT transcription, which makes MYCN amplification a route to telomerase activation rather than a separate telomere maintenance mechanism. TERT expression was higher in MYCN-amplified tumours, and in a MYCN-amplified cell line TERT was the gene most strongly downregulated when MYCN was knocked down. Not every MYCN-amplified tumour takes this route: some express TERT as low as ALT tumours do, and forced MYCN overexpression did not induce TERT where the promoter was repressed.

PMID:41560679 SUPPORT BACKGROUND Human Clinical
"MYCN amplification is a key factor contributing to the poor prognosis of NB."
Supports MYCN amplification as a key contributor to poor prognosis. The sentence is background in the abstract of an iPSC-derived neural crest model study, not a result of it; the patient-derived stage association is the Brodeur item below.
PMID:6719137 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Furthermore, N-myc amplification is highly correlated with advanced stages of disease (P less than 0.001) and with the ability to grow in vitro as an established cell line, both of which are associated with a poor prognosis."
Human clinical support for the aggressive-phenotype and poor-prognosis claim: in untreated primary tumors, MYCN amplification was absent in all 15 stage 1-2 cases and present in 50% of stage 3-4 cases.
PMID:29379199 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT In Vitro
"At oncogenic levels, MYCN associates with E-box binding motifs in an affinity-dependent manner, binding to strong canonical E-boxes at promoters and invading abundant weaker non-canonical E-boxes clustered at enhancers. Loss of MYCN leads to a global reduction in transcription, which is most..."
Supports the molecular function bound on this node. ChIP-seq in MYCN-amplified human neuroblastoma cell lines places MYCN on E-box motifs at promoters and enhancers, and switching MYCN off in an engineered tet-off neuroblastoma line lowers transcription, most at the target genes with the greatest enhancer occupancy. That is sequence-specific binding in cis-regulatory regions that modulates target-gene transcription, the two parts of DNA-binding transcription factor activity. Cell-line evidence only; the INCREASED modifier rests on the amplification evidence on this node, since this quote shows the activity rather than its level.

ALK Signaling Activation
ALK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase) is activated by point mutations in approximately 8-10% of neuroblastomas at diagnosis, and by amplification in additional cases. In neuroblastoma cells, high expression of the wild-type receptor can also lead to its constitutive activation. ALK mutations are enriched in familial neuroblastoma and represent a therapeutic target for ALK inhibitors.

Telomerase Activation
Telomerase-mediated telomere maintenance, one of the two telomere maintenance mechanisms in neuroblastoma. TERT rearrangements at 5p15.33 juxtapose the TERT coding sequence to strong enhancer elements, with chromatin remodelling and DNA methylation of the affected region, and despite their structural diversity they all induced massive transcriptional upregulation of TERT. MYCN amplification raises TERT transcription, and some tumours have high TERT expression with neither alteration. In 457 pretreatment neuroblastomas, TERT rearrangement was found in 46 and MYCN amplification in 93, and high TERT expression without either in 10 of 223 tumours with expression data. TERT promoter mutations are rare: none was found in 131 primary tumours representing the whole spectrum of the disease, and a single-centre series found them in 17 of 603 tumours. Activated telomerase, defined by these routes, was associated with the poorest overall survival and was an independent prognostic marker in multivariable analyses. Enzymatic telomerase activity has been shown in neuroblastoma cell lines that carry a TERT rearrangement or MYCN amplification.

PMID:26466568 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Despite a large structural diversity of these rearrangements, they all induced massive transcriptional upregulation of TERT."
Abstract result in patient tumours (whole-genome sequencing of 56, an extended series of 217, plus expression profiling): the TERT rearrangements were structurally diverse, yet all came with massive transcriptional upregulation of TERT. 'All' can only cover rearranged tumours with expression data, such as the 10 in the transcriptome comparison; 28 rearrangements were detected. 'Induced' is the authors' causal reading, backed by enhancer juxtaposition and TERT mRNA not tracking copy number, not by engineering a rearrangement. The quote concerns TERT mRNA; telomerase enzyme activity was measured only in cell lines.
PMID:26466568 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"The 5p15.33 rearrangements juxtapose the TERT coding sequence to strong enhancer elements, resulting in massive chromatin remodelling and DNA methylation of the affected region."
This abstract sentence summarises the paper's own results, mainly from patient tumour tissue: 5p15.33 rearrangements place TERT next to strong enhancer elements, with chromatin remodelling and DNA methylation of the affected region. The enhancer mapping rested on ChIP-seq of only three TERT-rearranged tumours, and part of the histone-mark survey used cell lines. The rise in CpG methylation across the TERT locus, measured in 39 primary tumours (six rearranged), was also seen in MYCN-amplified tumours, so it is not specific to rearrangement.
PMID:35100718 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"We detected TERT rearrangements in 46 of 457 cases (10.1%), MYCN amplification in 93 of 457 cases (20.4%), and elevated TERT expression in tumors lacking TERT or MYCN alterations in 10 of 223 cases (4.5%)."
In a series of 457 pretreatment neuroblastomas, the study found TERT rearrangement in 46 and MYCN amplification in 93 by fluorescence in situ hybridization, and elevated TERT expression without either alteration in 10 of 223 tumours profiled by microarray, a subset of the 273 also examined for ALT. The denominators differ, so the three percentages cannot be added together. The sentence itself does not mention telomerase: the authors class these alterations as activated telomerase in a later sentence, and the abstract reports no telomerase-activity assay on the tumours.
+ 5 more references
Reduced ATRX/DAXX Complex Abundance
Reduced abundance of the ATRX/DAXX chromatin remodelling complex, a recurrent molecular feature of alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) in neuroblastoma. ATRX encodes an ATP-dependent helicase of the SWI/SNF family of chromatin remodellers and, with DAXX, deposits the histone variant H3.3 at telomeric regions. ALT-positive neuroblastomas show reduced ATRX/DAXX complex abundance, due either to ATRX mutation (55% of them in one cohort) or to low protein expression, while mutations in the complex members DAXX and H3F3A were extremely rare. In a pooled analysis of published ATRX-altered neuroblastomas, 68% of ATRX aberrations were multi-exon deletions, and 75% of these were predicted to be in-frame. ATRX mutation is strongly age-dependent: in 104 patients with metastatic disease, sampled to represent each age group, it was found in tumours from 14 of 32 adolescents and young adults, 9 of 54 children and none of 18 infants, although infant cases are reported. In the pooled analysis, each of the three types of ATRX aberration was more frequent in patients diagnosed at an older age, yet about 40% of the ATRX-aberrant patients were five years or younger at diagnosis.

Downstream
Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres Loss of ATRX/DAXX complex function permits alternative lengthening of telomeres. ATRX mutation is associated with loss of nuclear ATRX protein and with ALT, and in one series every ALT tumour carried an ATRX or DAXX alteration. Without ATRX, histone H3.3 is not efficiently deposited at telomeric repeats, replication forks stall there, and the telomeres undergo the homologous recombination that leads to ALT.

Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres
Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), the recombination-based telomere maintenance mechanism that works without telomerase. Its measured frequency depends on cohort and assay: C-circle screening classified 9.2% of a 720-tumour screening cohort as ALT-positive, ALT-associated PML nuclear bodies marked 49 of 273 pretreatment neuroblastomas, and the C-circle assay marked 25 of 107 high-risk tumours from patients older than 18 months. In a registry cohort of 40 relapsed tumours, 47.5% were ALT-positive. ATRX alterations are found in only about half to 60% of ALT tumours. In primary tumours, ALT and the routes to telomerase activation occur almost mutually exclusively, and ATRX mutation and MYCN amplification co-occurred in only 1 of 819 tumours. ALT-positive neuroblastomas proliferate slowly, with a protracted clinical course, yet children with these tumours have a dismal outcome. About a third of ALT-positive tumours present with localized disease classified as low or intermediate risk, and in one cohort survival did not differ between ALT-positive tumours classified high risk and those classified low or intermediate risk.

PMID:32291317 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"ALT was identified in 23.4% of high-risk neuroblastoma tumors and genomic alterations in ATRX were detected in 60% of ALT tumors; 40% of ALT tumors lacked genomic alterations in known ALT-associated genes."
In a Children's Oncology Group cohort of patient primary tumours taken at diagnosis, this abstract sentence states the paper's own result: C-circle-defined ALT in 23.4% of high-risk tumours, with ATRX alterations in 60% of ALT tumours. The other 40% were ATRX wild-type by Sanger sequencing, and no DAXX, H3F3A or SMARCAL1 alteration was detected in them. The 60% (15 of 25) includes two cases called only from RNA-seq overexpression of in-frame-fusion ATRX transcripts; DNA sequencing alone found ATRX alterations in 13 of 23 sequenced ALT tumours (57%).

Unlimited Replicative Potential
The ability of tumour cells to keep dividing indefinitely, which a telomere maintenance mechanism (telomerase activation or ALT) provides. Its binding, increased cell population proliferation, follows the module node it conforms to and means expansion continuing past the limit that telomere shortening sets on normal cells, not a faster division rate: ALT-positive neuroblastomas proliferate more slowly than telomerase-activated ones. Aggressive neuroblastomas show a prolonged evolution during which they acquire telomere maintenance mechanisms, whereas tumours with a favourable prognosis expand clonally after a short evolution. In pretreatment neuroblastomas, patients whose tumours lacked a telomere maintenance mechanism had an excellent prognosis and those whose tumours had one did substantially worse. Within high-risk disease the picture is less clear: in one cohort the telomere maintenance groups differed in overall but not in event-free survival, and a subset of high-risk tumours lacks significant telomere lengthening activity, with cells derived from them proliferating for more than 200 population doublings while their telomeres shortened.

Histopathology

Schwannian Stroma-Poor Neuroblastic Histology
The defining histology of this entry under the International Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification (INPC), which the International Neuroblastoma Pathology Committee proposed in 1999 on the framework of the Shimada classification with minor modifications. INPC is an age-linked classification that depends on the differentiation grade of the neuroblasts, their cellular turnover index and the presence or absence of Schwannian stromal development. It places peripheral neuroblastic tumors in four categories: neuroblastoma (Schwannian stroma-poor), subtyped as undifferentiated, poorly differentiated or differentiating; ganglioneuroblastoma, intermixed (Schwannian stroma-rich); ganglioneuroma (Schwannian stroma-dominant); and ganglioneuroblastoma, nodular. Only the stroma-poor neuroblastoma category belongs to this entry. INPC was designed for prognostic distinction among pediatric peripheral neuroblastic tumors and is not applicable to adult ones, although there is no clear consensus on the age that separates the two groups.

Undifferentiated Neuroblastoma Subtype VERY_RARE
INPC subtype of the neuroblastoma category composed of tumor cells without clearly recognizable neurite production. Accordingly, in routine practice the diagnosis is confirmed by immunohistochemistry, in which positive nuclear staining for PHOX2B is critical. INPC classifies every neuroblastoma of the undifferentiated subtype as unfavorable histology, regardless of the patient's age. It is the rarest subtype: 177 of 4,680 Schwannian stroma-poor tumors (3.8%) classified at central review in the Children's Oncology Group Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory between August 2001 and March 2012, on specimens obtained before chemotherapy or irradiation.

Poorly Differentiated Neuroblastoma Subtype VERY_FREQUENT
INPC subtype in which the tumor cells produce neurites, with or without Homer Wright rosette formation, detectable on H&E staining; neuropil is present, but fewer than 5% of tumor cells show ganglionic differentiation. By differentiation grade, INPC places it in favorable histology when the patient is diagnosed younger than 18 months (up to 547 days) and in unfavorable histology from 18 months (548 days); a favorable assignment also requires a low or intermediate mitosis-karyorrhexis index (see INPC Favorable Histology). It is the commonest subtype: 4,081 of 4,680 Schwannian stroma-poor tumors (87.2%) classified at central review in the Children's Oncology Group Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory between August 2001 and March 2012.

Differentiating Neuroblastoma Subtype OCCASIONAL
INPC subtype in which more than 5% of tumor cells have the appearance of differentiating neuroblasts, defined by synchronous nuclear and cytoplasmic differentiation: cytoplasmic and nuclear enlargement, a cytoplasmic diameter at least twice the nuclear diameter, and an eccentrically located nucleus with vesicular chromatin and a single prominent nucleolus. Mitosis-Karyorrhexis Index
An INPC morphologic indicator for tumors in the neuroblastoma category: the number of mitotic and karyorrhectic cells per 5,000 neuroblastoma cells, classed as low (under 100), intermediate (100 to 200) or high (over 200). At the Children's Oncology Group Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory it is determined on primary or metastatic tumor samples submitted before chemotherapy or irradiation, excluding bone-marrow metastases. The prognostic meaning of low and intermediate MKI depends on age at diagnosis: among 4,282 neuroblastomas reviewed at that laboratory between August 2001 and March 2012, the INPC age cut-offs of 60 months for low MKI and 18 months for intermediate MKI were independently prognostic in multivariable analysis, whereas a 4-month cut-off within high MKI was not significant after adjustment, consistent with the INPC applying no age cut-off to high MKI. In a Children's Cancer Group series reported in 2001, MYCN-amplified neuroblastomas lacked neuroblastic differentiation regardless of patient age and were generally linked to increased mitotic and karyorrhectic activity, with higher MKI classes in younger patients.

INPC Favorable Histology
The INPC favorable-histology group as defined for the neuroblastoma category: poorly differentiated or differentiating tumors with a low or intermediate mitosis-karyorrhexis index in patients younger than 18 months, and differentiating tumors with a low index in patients aged 18 months to 5 years. Among 630 neuroblastoma-category tumors in a Children's Cancer Group pathology review reported in 2001, this subgroup had 90.4% 5-year event-free survival. Under the INPC the grouping is to be determined only from primary or metastatic tumor tissue obtained before chemotherapy or irradiation, and once assigned it is not to be changed during the clinical course, because therapy-associated histologic changes may not have proven prognostic significance. The Children's Oncology Group and International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) classifications use INPC histology differently: the Children's Oncology Group stratifies treatment using age together with histology classified by the age-linked INPC criteria, which by definition duplicates the prognostic contribution of age, whereas the INRG classification incorporates individual histologic features underlying INPC. A 2020 analysis of the INRG Data Commons recommended replacing INPC with those individual features in the Children's Oncology Group classification as well; that was a proposal, and when it was published the Children's Oncology Group classification still combined INPC histology with age.

INPC Unfavorable Histology
The INPC unfavorable-histology group as defined for the neuroblastoma category: undifferentiated tumors and tumors with a high mitosis-karyorrhexis index at any age; poorly differentiated tumors, and tumors with an intermediate index, in patients aged 18 months to 5 years; and any neuroblastoma-category tumor in patients aged 5 years or older. That figure belongs to its cohort and era: a 2022 review gives 5-year event-free survival of 54.6% for unfavorable and 88.1% for favorable histology (5-year overall survival 65.6% and 96.4%), citing the cohort analyzed for the 2021 revised Children's Oncology Group risk classification. In high-risk disease, histology after induction chemotherapy differs from the diagnostic histology, but the difference has not been shown to be prognostic: in paired diagnostic and post-induction resection samples from 94 high-risk patients on Children's Oncology Group trials (2001-2013), tumors resected after induction chemotherapy had shifted toward a more differentiated, less mitotically active histology, and neither histologic features at resection nor their change from diagnosis was significantly associated with progression-free or overall survival.

Context-specific annotations (1)
Children with neuroblastoma and spinal canal invasion in the SIOPEN prospective multinational NB-SCI study (196 evaluable patients)
A cohort selected for spinal canal invasion, which the study defines as tumor growth through the neural foramina into the spinal canal, so the proportions below are conditional on intraspinal extension, not rates for neuroblastoma as a whole. Of the 208 patients registered, 196 were evaluable; 67% were symptomatic and 33% asymptomatic at enrollment. Symptomatic means any symptom attributed to the spinal canal invasion and recorded with standardized measures (motor deficit, pain, sensory deficit, bladder or bowel dysfunction, spine deformity or dyspnea), which is somewhat broader than signs of cord compression alone, so the symptomatic proportion is not recorded as a frequency of spinal cord compression. The cohort also includes tumors the authors class as histologically benign (ganglioneuroma, intermixed ganglioneuroblastoma) and a few patients enrolled at relapse. The asymptomatic share shows that tumor in the spinal canal does not always cause clinical compression; such asymptomatic extension is not counted in the registry rate given in the phenotype's main evidence.

PMID:3002599 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Serum neuron-specific enolase (NSE) was measured in 61 children at diagnosis with all stages of neuroblastoma. The median serum values for Stages I, II, III, IV, and IV-S were 13, 23, 40, 214, and 40 ng/ml, respectively. ... In patients with Stages III and IV disease, a raised serum NSE level..."
In a series of 61 children with neuroblastoma of all stages, sampled at diagnosis, median serum NSE was 13, 23, 40 and 214 ng/ml in stages I, II, III and IV, and 40 ng/ml in stage IV-S. The authors report stage IV-S levels as significantly lower than stage IV levels despite extensive tumor burden, so serum NSE does not simply track tumor burden. In stage III and IV disease, 1 of 19 patients (5%) with NSE above 100 ng/ml survived, against 5 of 8 (63%) with values below 100 ng/ml. Limitations: this comparison rests on 19 patients above and 8 below the cut-off, and the abstract gives no significance test for it and does not report it within stage III or stage IV separately, so from the abstract the effect of NSE cannot be separated from that of stage. Staging follows the Roman-numeral system then in use (stages I to IV and IV-S), and the 100 ng/ml cut-off was set with an assay of that era and may not transfer to current immunoassays.
PMID:6135871 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical

In a Children's Cancer Study Group series of 122 children with stage IV neuroblastoma sampled at diagnosis, 96% had serum NSE more than three standard deviations above the mean for age-matched normal children, and survival analysis suggested that levels above 100 ng/ml were associated with poor outcome. The abstract reports this relation as highly significant in the subgroup of infants under 1 year at diagnosis (all 7 below 100 ng/ml alive up to 36 months; 7 of 8 above it dead within 12 months) and gives no significance level for the stage IV group as a whole. It therefore supports raised NSE in stage IV disease only, not in neuroblastoma generally. Its stage IV finding is consistent with the 100 ng/ml threshold that PMID:3002599 reported for stage III and IV disease combined, but the studies share their lead authors, so their patients may overlap and they are not independent replications.

Diagnosis

3
123I-MIBG Scintigraphy
Whole-body scintigraphy with iodine-123-labelled metaiodobenzylguanidine (123I-MIBG), the functional imaging test for staging and response assessment. In its 2010 guideline on MIBG scans, the INRG Task Force called 123I-MIBG the radiopharmaceutical of choice in children, and MIBG scans, particularly with a semi-quantitative score, the most sensitive and specific method of staging and response evaluation. The INRG staging system makes 123I-MIBG scintigraphy mandatory, preferably before tumor excision. Under the 2017 revised International Neuroblastoma Response Criteria (INRC), response is assessed with anatomic imaging, 123I-MIBG or FDG-PET, and bilateral bone marrow aspirates and trephine biopsies; 123I-MIBG replaces technetium-99m bone scintigraphy at osteomedullary lesions, and skeletal uptake is scored relative to baseline with the same scoring method (for example Curie or SIOPEN) at each time point. In a prospective multicenter trial of patients with known or suspected neuroblastoma, 123I-MIBG scintigraphy had a sensitivity of 88% and a specificity of 83%. A 2024 systematic review of ten head-to-head studies found that PET/CT with catecholaminergic tracers (11C-HED, 18F-DOPA, 124I-MIBG or 18F-mFBG) detected significantly more lesions than MIBG scintigraphy in seven of them but was superior per patient in only two; the authors judged PET diagnostically superior but said its effect on clinical decisions was unknown, and noted that these tracers were rarely used in clinical practice and not included in new high-risk treatment protocols. Drugs can interfere with MIBG uptake: labetalol, which is usually effective for neuroblastoma-associated hypertension, must be stopped for several days before MIBG is given, and a tumor without MIBG uptake should raise the question of interfering medication, although complete blockade of uptake is rare.

18F-FDG PET/CT for MIBG-Nonavid Disease
18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/CT, which the 2017 revised INRC use in place of 123I-MIBG when the tumor does not concentrate MIBG: FDG-PET or PET/CT for tumor detection in bone, and FDG-PET as an alternative modality for assessing primary or metastatic soft tissue and bony sites. FDG is less specific than MIBG, because inflammatory lesions and normal or cytokine-stimulated bone marrow also take it up, so the INRC add that a biopsy of at least one FDG-avid, MIBG-nonavid lesion may be required to confirm neuroblastoma or ganglioneuroblastoma. The earlier INRG documents named bone scintigraphy, not FDG-PET, for skeletal assessment in these patients: the 2009 INRG staging system requires technetium-99m bone scintigraphy, at any age, when MIBG positivity of the primary tumor cannot be confirmed because the primary has been removed or is not MIBG-avid, and the 2010 INRG Task Force MIBG guideline called the technetium-99m MDP bone scan the standard test for skeletal metastases in tumors negative for MIBG at diagnosis. That guideline considered investigating alternatives preferable, because the bone scan has low specificity and is hard to interpret in young children with growing bones, but judged the clinical value of FDG-PET not yet well defined and its routine use, especially as a substitute for 123I-MIBG scintigraphy, not justified. A 2015 Cochrane review advised an additional test, such as FDG-PET(-CT), for staging and response assessment in patients whose tumor does not accumulate 123I-MIBG, while noting that more evidence of its clinical value was needed. The 2018 EANM guideline covers PET/CT with 18F-FDG, 18F-DOPA and 68Ga-DOTA peptides and describes these studies as increasingly used in clinical practice.

Urinary Catecholamine Metabolites
Measurement of catecholamine metabolites in urine, chiefly vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and homovanillic acid (HVA). Under the INSS diagnostic criteria used by the INRG classification system, neuroblastoma can be diagnosed from unequivocal tumor cells in bone marrow together with increased urine or serum catecholamines or metabolites, as an alternative to a diagnosis from tumor tissue. The 2017 revised INRC do not use urine catecholamine levels to evaluate response, because specimen collection and analysis are not standardized and diet influences the results; the same consensus statement names catecholamine levels, with bone scintigraphy, as examples of tumor-assessment modalities less sensitive and/or specific for neuroblastoma, which the revision set out to replace with 123I-MIBG and FDG-PET imaging. Studies comparing urinary catecholamines with bone marrow studies and MIBG scans have found HVA and VMA to have low sensitivity as markers for monitoring disease activity. In a retrospective high-risk cohort, however, positive status on an extended panel of eight urinary catecholamine metabolites at complete remission was associated with poorer event-free and overall survival. The frequency of raised VMA and HVA at diagnosis is recorded under the biochemical record Catecholamine Metabolites.

Imaging Findings

2
MIBG-Avid Disease VERY_FREQUENT
Uptake of MIBG at the sites of disease, primary and metastatic, on 123I-MIBG scintigraphy. Neuroblastoma cells typically express the norepinephrine transporter (NET), which mediates active MIBG uptake in about 90% of patients; in a Cochrane review, about 10% of histologically proven neuroblastomas did not accumulate 123I-MIBG (recorded separately as MIBG-Nonavid Disease). In a small COG series of high-risk patients, the percentage of tumor cells expressing NET protein was higher in avid than nonavid tumors (P = 0.027), but the groups overlapped widely, including an avid tumor with no NET-expressing cells; NET mRNA measured by quantitative PCR did not differ significantly (P = 0.31), and neither did VMAT1 or VMAT2 mRNA. In a later COG immunohistochemistry study of tumors from 76 patients with high-risk metastatic disease, avid tumors had higher composite VMAT2 protein scores than nonavid tumors (median 216 vs 45, P = 0.04), with substantial overlap between the groups, while VMAT1 protein showed no association. In a 23-patient expression-array subset of a 343-patient COG cohort, NET mRNA was lower in nonavid tumors at borderline significance (P = 0.052) while VMAT2 mRNA did not differ; the authors note that this NET result is contrary to their earlier PCR result and may reflect differences in methodology or tumor material.

modality is OTHER because the whole-body survey in 123I-MIBG imaging is planar scintigraphy, which ImagingModalityEnum does not list. SPECT or SPECT/CT, which the enum does list, is often added over selected regions, such as the chest and abdomen or sites where tumor must be told apart from physiological uptake, and does not replace the whole-body images. NCIT:C79553 is specific to 123I-MIBG, the INRG Task Force's radiopharmaceutical of choice in children; two of the COG transporter studies cited here (PMID:23050139, PMID:26338179) read avidity from diagnostic 123I- or 131I-MIBG scans obtained by local institutional practice, and the third (PMID:28383813) does not state the isotope. NCIT has no isotope-neutral or 131I uptake finding to bind instead: OLS NCIT searches on 2026-10-21 for "MIBG uptake" and "MIBG scintigraphy" returned NCIT:C79553 as the only finding term, "131I-MIBG" returned only the tracer NCIT:C970 Iobenguane I-131, and "MIBG avid" returned nothing.

MIBG-Nonavid Disease OCCASIONAL
Tumor that does not take up MIBG on diagnostic scintigraphy, so that the MIBG scan is falsely negative. In a Cochrane review, about 10% of histologically proven neuroblastomas did not accumulate 123I-MIBG. The INRG Task Force attributes such false-negative scans to low norepinephrine transporter expression, the blood-brain barrier, or large areas of scar or necrosis, while the Cochrane authors judged the reasons not entirely clear, suggesting that altered uptake mechanisms or interfering medication may contribute. In a COG cohort of 343 patients with metastatic high- or intermediate-risk disease, 30 (8.7%) were MIBG-nonavid at diagnosis. Compared with patients with avid disease, they less often had adrenal primary tumors or bone metastases, less often had positive urine catecholamines (compared in the high-risk patients only), more often had MYCN-amplified tumors (a difference significant in the pooled cohort but not among the high-risk patients alone), and had better 5-year event-free survival. On multivariable analysis among the high-risk patients, avidity was the only adverse prognostic factor for event-free survival identified (hazard ratio 1.77 for avid versus nonavid disease; P = 0.034); in the pooled cohort the adjusted hazard ratio was not significant (P = 0.059).

INRGSS Stage MS
Metastatic disease in a child younger than 18 months (547 days) with metastases confined to skin, liver and/or bone marrow, bone marrow involvement below 10% of nucleated cells, and meta-iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scintigraphy negative in bone and bone marrow; the primary tumor may be L1 or L2, with no restriction on crossing or infiltrating the midline. INSS stage 4S is the narrower INSS counterpart, limited to infants younger than 12 months with an INSS stage 1 or 2 primary tumor and dissemination to liver, skin and/or bone marrow (under 10% involvement); the INRGSS extended the age limit to 18 months and admitted primaries infiltrating the midline (INSS stage 3). In an Italian series of 30 infants with stage IV-S disease treated in 1970-1981, the liver was the most frequent site of spread (87%), and subcutaneous nodules were recorded. In infants with stage IV-S or 4S disease the pattern is associated with spontaneous regression and good survival. In two infant cohorts, one limited to symptomatic or biologically unfavorable cases, most deaths occurred in infants younger than 2 months at diagnosis, most often from complications of hepatomegaly or extensive abdominal involvement. In the selected cohort, enrolled on the COG trial ANBL0531, no further deaths from hepatomegaly occurred after the protocol was amended to require immediate chemotherapy for infants younger than 2 months with evolving hepatomegaly. In a Children's Oncology Group cohort staged by the INRGSS, stage MS outcome was excellent except for MYCN-amplified tumors, which have a poor outcome. Whether toddlers aged 12 to 18 months with a 4S pattern of metastasis share the favorable outcome of infants is contested. In the INRG database, toddlers grouped by metastatic sites alone, without the marrow limit of stage MS, had worse event-free survival than infants with the 4S pattern and outcomes similar to stage 4 disease at the same age, and the authors concluded that tumor biology matters more than age or metastatic pattern. Registry data from two Japanese pediatric societies showed an excellent prognosis for stage 4s disease at 12 to 17 months.
INSS stage 4S is recorded within this stage, not as a has_subtypes row, because the cancer granularity ladder (design decisions §3a) records stage under stages. The 4S category descends from the IV-S category of the 1971 Evans staging system, recognizing patients with metastatic disease limited to skin, liver and bone marrow who have superior outcomes, and the 1993 revision of the INSS added restrictions on age and bone marrow involvement for stage 4S. When the INRG Task Force extended the age limit to 18 months, it described the group aged 12 to 18 months as small, with an unclear outcome.

Age-standardised incidence rate of 10.9 cases per million children in 1988-1997, highest in infants (52.6 per million). The authors suggest that some overdiagnosis in children under 2 years may explain the rise in incidence over 1978-1997. The abstract states the rate per million children without a time unit, recorded here as annual, the usual convention for registry age-standardised rates, and does not say whether ganglioneuroblastoma is counted.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:16919772 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"The age-standardised incidence rate (ASR) of neuroblastoma in Europe in 1988-1997 was 10.9 cases per million children, being highest in infants (52.6)."
The ACCIS report, which pools European population-based childhood cancer registry data, gives the 1988-1997 age-standardised incidence rate of neuroblastoma in Europe as 10.9 cases per million children (1.09 per 100,000), highest in infants at 52.6 per million. The abstract states the rate per million children without a time unit, and gives the 0-14 year age span only indirectly, by describing older children as aged 2-14 years. It does not say whether ganglioneuroblastoma is counted with neuroblastoma.
PMID:16919772 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"A certain amount of overdiagnosis in children under 2 years of age may explain the increased incidence rates and partially the increase in survival."
In the same registry analysis (6202 children with neuroblastoma from 59 registries in 19 countries, 1978-1997), the authors suggest that some overdiagnosis in children under 2 years of age may explain the increased incidence rates, so the European rate may be inflated in the youngest children. They hedge (may explain) and do not estimate how much of the rise overdiagnosis accounts for.
Quebec and the Greater Delaware Valley, children under 15 years
Annual Incidence 1.095 per 100,000 per year 1–9 per 100,000 per year
Population-based series pooling Quebec (Canada) and the area covered by the Greater Delaware Valley Pediatric Tumor Registry (United States): 295 children with neuroblastoma in a combined population of 3,178,736 children. Annual incidence was 10.95 per million under 15 years and 27.75 per million at ages 0-4 years. The Quebec data were collected shortly before province-wide screening began. The abstract gives no years of diagnosis and does not say whether ganglioneuroblastoma is counted.

PMID:1732433 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"One hundred thirty children with neuroblastoma were identified in Quebec and 165 in the GDV, in a combined population of 3,178,736 children. The annual incidence of neuroblastoma was 10.95/10(6) under the age of 15 years and 27.75/10(6) between the ages of 0 and 4 years."
Primary result of this population-based study. The first quoted sentence gives the study population: 130 children with neuroblastoma in Quebec and 165 in the Greater Delaware Valley (GDV), whose pediatric tumor registry covers all of Delaware and parts of New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Maryland, in a combined population of 3,178,736 children. The second gives the annual incidence in that population: 10.95 per million children under 15 years (1.095 per 100,000) and 27.75 per million at ages 0-4. The Quebec data come from shortly before province-wide screening began. The abstract gives no years of diagnosis and does not say whether ganglioneuroblastoma was counted.
Australia, children aged 0-14 years (Australian Childhood Cancer Registry, 1983-2015)
Annual Incidence 0.95 per 100,000 per year 1–9 per 1,000,000 per year
Age-standardised incidence of about 9.5 per million children per year, steady across 1983-2015. The study counted neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroblastoma together, so the rate covers a broader group of tumors than this entry; the abstract does not say how many of the 1269 patients had ganglioneuroblastoma.

PMID:32068329 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Age-standardised incidence rates remained steady across the study period at approximately 9.5 per million children per year."
National population-based study of Australian Childhood Cancer Registry data for children aged 0-14 years diagnosed from 1983 to 2015: age-standardised incidence remained steady across the period at approximately 9.5 per million children per year (0.95 per 100,000). The registry extract covered neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroblastoma together and the abstract gives no separate rate for either, so the figure applies to the combined group. The abstract does not name the standard population used for age-standardisation.
PMID:32068329 SUPPORT INDIRECT Human Clinical
"Deidentified data for all children (0-14 years) diagnosed with neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroblastoma from 1983 to 2015 were extracted."
The abstract's methods define the study cohort as all children aged 0-14 years diagnosed with neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroblastoma from 1983 to 2015, and its results report that cohort's incidence of about 9.5 per million children per year without restating the case definition, so reading the rate as covering both tumor types is an inference from the abstract's structure. Ganglioneuroblastoma is outside this entry, so it widens the rate's numerator, the cases counted; the denominator, Australian children aged 0-14 years, is unchanged.
Germany, children aged 0-14 years (German Childhood Cancer Registry, 1980-2015)
Annual Incidence 1.32 per 100,000 per year 1–9 per 100,000 per year
Median of the annual age-standardised incidence rates (Segi world standard) over 1980-2015: 13.2 per million children per year, ranging from 8.7 in 1981 (incomplete registration) to 17.8 in 2000 (the last year of the screening trial). Urine screening for catecholamine metabolites was offered at about 1 year of age in 6 of 16 German states from 1995 to 2000, and incidence in those years ran above the long-term trend (rate ratio 1.26). The paper does not say whether ganglioneuroblastoma is counted with neuroblastoma.

PMID:28786082 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"The population-based median annual age standardized incidence rate (ASR) of neuroblastoma per million children per year in Germany between the periods 1980 and 2015 was 13.2"
The authors' population-based analysis of German Childhood Cancer Registry data gives the median of the annual age-standardised incidence rates (Segi world standard) for 1980-2015 as 13.2 neuroblastoma cases per million children per year, which is 1.32 per 100,000. It is a median of annual rates, not a pooled rate for the period, and the paper's Figure 1 gives the age band as 0-14 years. The same sentence goes on to give the extremes, 8.7 per million in 1981 (incomplete registration) and 17.8 in 2000 (the last year of the screening trial); the Methods add that case numbers before 1986 were not complete enough for epidemiological analysis, although the median spans 1980-2015. The paper does not say whether ganglioneuroblastoma is counted with neuroblastoma.
PMID:28786082 SUPPORT INDIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"The age-adjusted regression curve (Fig. 1) shows an increase in crude neuroblastoma incidence rates during the period of neuroblastoma screening (RR 1.26; 95% CI 1.17-1.36)"
The authors' age-adjusted trend analysis of German registry incidence in children aged 0-14 (trend fitted to 1986-2014 and adjusted for age distribution, German reunification and the screening trial) found crude incidence during the screening period raised by a rate ratio of 1.26 (95% CI 1.17-1.36) relative to the fitted trend. A median taken over 1980-2015 therefore includes these raised years. The rate ratio is a deviation from the fitted trend, not a comparison with a fixed pre-screening baseline, and it is a national estimate although screening was offered in only some states.
PMID:28786082 SUPPORT BACKGROUND Human Clinical
"Urine screening for catecholamine metabolites to detect early neuroblastoma was offered to children at approximately 1 year of age in 6 of 16 German States from 1995 to 2000"
Gives the dates and scope of the screening period: urine screening for catecholamine metabolites was offered at about 1 year of age in 6 of 16 German states from 1995 to 2000. This Methods sentence describes a programme reported separately (the paper's reference 11) and says nothing about incidence; the rate ratio comes from the Results sentence above.
Europe
Point Prevalence 10.0–50.0 per 100,000 1–9 per 10,000
Orphanet point-prevalence class for Europe, 1-5 per 10,000, which Orphadata attributes to a 2018 European Medicines Agency document. A point prevalence counts everyone living with the disease at one time, so it is not comparable with the childhood incidence records above.

Orphanet's epidemiology table for ORPHA:635 gives a point-prevalence class of 1-5 per 10,000 for Europe. It is a coarse class for the whole population, not a rate measured in a defined cohort. Epidemiology

2
Proportion of childhood cancers
Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood, accounting for about 8-10% of childhood cancers and about 15% of childhood cancer deaths. In Canadian incidence data for 1982-1986 and 1987-1991 it accounted for a larger share of cancers in the first year of life than any other cancer.
Show evidence (3 references)
PMID:39720601 SUPPORT DIRECT BACKGROUND Human Clinical
"Neuroblastoma is the most prevalent extracranial solid tumor in pediatric populations worldwide, representing 8-10% of childhood malignancies and contributing to approximately 15% of pediatric cancer-related fatalities."
The first sentence of the abstract's BACKGROUND section states the first three claims of this item: neuroblastoma is the most frequent extracranial solid tumor of childhood (the abstract's word is most prevalent), accounts for 8-10% of childhood malignancies, and accounts for about 15% of childhood cancer deaths. These are established figures that the paper's introduction attributes to earlier publications (its references 1-3), not results of its own Global Burden of Disease analysis.
PMID:28846355 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human Clinical
"Neuroblastoma represents the most common extracranial solid tumor in childhood and primarily affects very young children."
A StatPearls review chapter stating that neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood. It supports only that clause; the shares of childhood cancers and of childhood cancer deaths rest on the item above.
PMID:9328197 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"The age-specific distributions of incident cancers indicate that neuroblastoma accounts for the greatest proportion of all cancers in children less than one year of age."
This analysis of childhood cancer incidence and mortality across Canada for 1982-86 and 1987-91 found, in its age-specific distribution of incident cancers, that neuroblastoma made up the largest share of all cancers diagnosed before age one. The quoted sentence does not repeat the country or the periods, which the abstract's opening sentence sets. The data are from 1982-1991, so this records the historical Canadian pattern rather than a current figure. MEDLINE indexes the paper under Ganglioneuroblastoma as well as Neuroblastoma, so its counts may include ganglioneuroblastoma; the abstract does not say.
Age at diagnosis
Neuroblastoma is diagnosed mainly in infancy and early childhood. In the Netherlands Cancer Registry (patients under 18 years diagnosed 1990-2014), 45% of 593 patients were younger than 18 months at diagnosis. In the German national trial cohort the median age at diagnosis fell from 23 months in 1980-1984 to 15 months in 2010-2014, and StatPearls gives a median of 17 months.
Show evidence (3 references)
PMID:31726247 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Of the 593 newly diagnosed neuroblastoma cases, 45% was <18 months of age at diagnosis and 52% had stage 4 disease."
This Netherlands Cancer Registry analysis took data on all patients aged under 18 years diagnosed with neuroblastoma from 1990 to 2014. Its own result is that 45% of the 593 newly diagnosed cases were younger than 18 months at diagnosis, a share of the whole cohort across all stages. The abstract gives only this 18-month split, not a fuller age distribution, and does not say whether ganglioneuroblastoma was counted.
PMID:28786082 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"The median age at diagnosis decreased from 23 months during 1980-1984 to 15 months during 2010-2014."
Result of the nationwide analysis of the German GPOH neuroblastoma trials NB79 to NB2004, whose patients were 96.6% of those known to the German Childhood Cancer Registry. Table 2 gives the all-stage median age at diagnosis as 22.7 months in 1980-84 and 15.1 months in 2010-14; the median had already reached 15.1 months by 1995-99. The authors attribute the fall mainly to earlier diagnosis of low- and intermediate-risk patients; the median for stage 4 patients aged 18 months or more stayed near 40 months. Trial coverage of registered patients was lower in the early 1980s, above 90% from 1985 and at least 98% from 1995.
PMID:28846355 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human Clinical
"The median age at diagnosis is 17 months"
The StatPearls chapter states that the median age at diagnosis is 17 months. It is a point-of-care review and the abstract does not name the cohort behind the median, so the figure is a synthesis rather than a primary measurement.

Animal Models

1
Xenopus anteroventral noradrenergic (AVNA) cell differentiation model Developmental model of the presumed cell of origin
Rather than growing a tumour, this model reconstructs the normal differentiation of the neural-crest-derived sympathoadrenal cell that neuroblastoma is thought to arise from, and asks what stops it. Frog AVNA cells differentiate under transient Ascl1 expression; in neuroblastoma cells Ascl1 is instead persistently expressed and multiply phosphorylated. Introducing that phospho-state into the frog cells blocks their differentiation, and CDK or MYCN overexpression blocks it too — but not when Ascl1 cannot be phosphorylated, which places phosphorylation downstream of both. The model tests the differentiation-arrest hypothesis in a normal developmental context; it does not produce tumours and so says nothing about transformation, growth, or metastasis.
Species
Xenopus laevis
Genotype
Embryos expressing wild-type Ascl1, a phospho-mutant Ascl1 that cannot be phosphorylated at serine-proline motifs, CDKs, or MYCN, with Ascl1 morpholino knockdown
Genes
ASCL1 hgnc:738 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this experimental model concerns this gene This experimental model concerns ASCL1 (hgnc:738). hgnc:738 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee. MYCN hgnc:7559 HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (hgnc) Relation: this experimental model concerns this gene This experimental model concerns MYCN (hgnc:7559). hgnc:7559 is a gene from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee.
Publication
PMID:25786414
Pathograph links
Neural Crest Developmental Arrest recapitulates fidelity: moderate Supplies a molecular switch for the arrest this node asserts: multi-site phosphorylation of Ascl1 converts it from a driver of sympathoadrenal differentiation into an inert factor, matching the phospho-state Ascl1 is held in within neuroblastoma cells.
Limitations: Frog AVNA cells are a developmental counterpart of the presumed cell of origin, not tumour cells, and the model contains no transformed tissue — arrest is scored as failure to differentiate on schedule rather than as tumour formation. The link to human disease rests on the observed phospho-state of ASCL1 in neuroblastoma lines, so the model shows the state is sufficient to block differentiation, not that it is what maintains any patient's tumour.
Readouts
AVNA cell differentiation driven by wild-type versus phospho-mutant Ascl1
Direction: DECREASED
Interpretation: Differentiation fails when Ascl1 can be multiply phosphorylated and proceeds when it cannot, isolating phospho-status as the controlling variable.

+ 1 more reference
MYCN-Driven Proliferation perturbs fidelity: moderate Positions MYCN upstream of the differentiation block: MYCN overexpression prevents Ascl1-driven differentiation, and loses that ability when Ascl1 cannot be phosphorylated.
Limitations: This is the differentiation-blocking arm of MYCN only. The node is about proliferation, and no proliferative or tumour-growth readout was taken here; MYCN is introduced by overexpression in a normal embryo, not by the genomic amplification that defines high-risk neuroblastoma.
Readouts
Ascl1-driven AVNA differentiation under CDK or MYCN overexpression
Direction: DECREASED
Interpretation: The epistasis result: MYCN and CDKs block differentiation only when Ascl1 is phosphorylatable, so their effect on this cell fate runs through Ascl1 phospho-status.

name: Neuroblastoma
creation_date: '2026-01-26T02:55:13Z'
description: >-
  Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood,
  arising from neural crest-derived sympathetic nervous system precursors.
  It demonstrates remarkable clinical heterogeneity, ranging from spontaneous
  regression in infants to highly aggressive metastatic disease in older
  children. MYCN amplification, present in approximately 20% of cases, is
  among the most powerful adverse genomic prognostic markers and drives
  aggressive tumor behavior. Risk stratification in the INRG system combines
  stage, age, histologic category and grade of differentiation, MYCN status,
  chromosome 11q status, and DNA ploidy to guide treatment intensity. A
  distinct axis of neuroblastoma biology is the mechanism of telomere
  maintenance: telomerase is activated through TERT rearrangement, MYCN
  amplification or high TERT expression without either alteration, while
  alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), often with ATRX alteration,
  maintains telomeres without telomerase. The two mechanisms are almost mutually
  exclusive. ATRX-altered disease is enriched in older children, adolescents and
  young adults and often runs a slow but progressive course, with poor response
  to induction chemotherapy reported for large ATRX deletions and truncating
  mutations.
  Low-risk neuroblastoma may require only observation, while high-risk
  disease requires intensive multimodal therapy with immunotherapy.
categories:
- Pediatric Cancer
- Neural Tumor
- Solid Tumor
parents:
- neuroblastic tumor
synonyms:
- neuroblastoma, malignant
- neuroblastoma (Schwannian stroma-poor)
- NB
notes: >-
  This entry covers neuroblastoma of the sympathoadrenal lineage of the neural
  crest, arising in the adrenal medulla or elsewhere along the sympathetic
  nervous system, which is the Schwannian stroma-poor category of the
  International Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification. MONDO defines
  MONDO:0005072 as an extracranial childhood cancer that originates from neural
  crest tissues of the sympathetic nervous system, and NCIT defines NCIT:C3270
  as a malignant neuroblastic tumor with neuroblastic cells, no ganglion cells
  and no prominent Schwannian stroma. Both classes nevertheless also contain
  tumors that this entry does not cover: olfactory neuroblastoma (MONDO:0006329,
  NCIT:C3789), which MONDO places under extracranial neuroblastoma
  (MONDO:0002749); cerebral neuroblastoma (MONDO:0002900), including CNS
  neuroblastoma with FOXR2 activation (MONDO:0859597, NCIT:C186547); and retinal
  neuroblastoma (MONDO:0024340, NCIT:C6956). Site-specific subclasses of
  peripheral disease, such as adrenal gland (MONDO:0006076), retroperitoneal
  (MONDO:0000551) and mediastinum (MONDO:0001095) neuroblastoma, are within
  scope, but the ganglioneuroblastoma classes that MONDO files beneath two of
  them, adrenal gland ganglioneuroblastoma (MONDO:0004477) and mediastinum
  ganglioneuroblastoma (MONDO:0001096), are not. Ganglioneuroblastoma
  (MONDO:0005035) and ganglioneuroma (MONDO:0005033), the other neuroblastic
  tumors under MONDO:0006316, are separate diseases. MONDO's neuroblastoma
  susceptibility classes, numbered 1 to 7 (MONDO:0009741, MONDO:0700041,
  MONDO:0013083, MONDO:0013084, MONDO:0013085, MONDO:0013086 and MONDO:0014774),
  are also outside this entry; MONDO files them under hereditary neoplastic
  syndrome (MONDO:0015356), not under MONDO:0005072. Registry incidence figures
  under prevalence may count ganglioneuroblastoma together with neuroblastoma;
  each record says what its source states.

    reference_title: "A population-based study of neuroblastoma incidence, survival, and mortality in North America."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "One hundred thirty children with neuroblastoma were identified in Quebec and 165 in the GDV, in a combined population of 3,178,736 children. The annual incidence of neuroblastoma was 10.95/10(6) under the age of 15 years and 27.75/10(6) between the ages of 0 and 4 years."
    explanation: >-
      Primary result of this population-based study. The first quoted sentence
      gives the study population: 130 children with neuroblastoma in Quebec and
      165 in the Greater Delaware Valley (GDV), whose pediatric tumor registry
      covers all of Delaware and parts of New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Maryland,
      in a combined population of 3,178,736 children. The second gives the
      annual incidence in that population: 10.95 per million children under 15
      years (1.095 per 100,000) and 27.75 per million at ages 0-4. The Quebec
      data come from shortly before province-wide screening began. The abstract
      gives no years of diagnosis and does not say whether ganglioneuroblastoma
      was counted.
- population: "Australia, children aged 0-14 years (Australian Childhood Cancer Registry, 1983-2015)"
  measure_type: ANNUAL_INCIDENCE
  prevalence_class: BAND_1_9_PER_1000000
  rate_per_100000: 0.95
  rate_denominator: POPULATION_PER_YEAR
  notes: >-
    Age-standardised incidence of about 9.5 per million children per year,
    steady across 1983-2015. The study counted neuroblastoma and
    ganglioneuroblastoma together, so the rate covers a broader group of tumors
    than this entry; the abstract does not say how many of the 1269 patients had
    ganglioneuroblastoma.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:32068329
    reference_title: "Incidence and outcomes of neuroblastoma in Australian children: A population-based study (1983-2015)."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL

    explanation: >-
      National population-based study of Australian Childhood Cancer Registry
      data for children aged 0-14 years diagnosed from 1983 to 2015:
      age-standardised incidence remained steady across the period at
      approximately 9.5 per million children per year (0.95 per 100,000). The
      registry extract covered neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroblastoma together
      and the abstract gives no separate rate for either, so the figure applies
      to the combined group. The abstract does not name the standard population
      used for age-standardisation.
  - reference: PMID:32068329
    reference_title: "Incidence and outcomes of neuroblastoma in Australian children: A population-based study (1983-2015)."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Deidentified data for all children (0-14 years) diagnosed with neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroblastoma from 1983 to 2015 were extracted."
    explanation: >-
      The abstract's methods define the study cohort as all children aged 0-14
      years diagnosed with neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroblastoma from 1983 to
      2015, and its results report that cohort's incidence of about 9.5 per
      million children per year without restating the case definition, so
      reading the rate as covering both tumor types is an inference from the
      abstract's structure. Ganglioneuroblastoma is outside this entry, so it
      widens the rate's numerator, the cases counted; the denominator,
      Australian children aged 0-14 years, is unchanged.
- population: "Germany, children aged 0-14 years (German Childhood Cancer Registry, 1980-2015)"
  measure_type: ANNUAL_INCIDENCE
  prevalence_class: BAND_1_9_PER_100000
  rate_per_100000: 1.32
  rate_denominator: POPULATION_PER_YEAR
  notes: >-
    Median of the annual age-standardised incidence rates (Segi world standard)
    over 1980-2015: 13.2 per million children per year, ranging from 8.7 in 1981
    (incomplete registration) to 17.8 in 2000 (the last year of the screening
    trial). Urine screening for catecholamine metabolites was offered at about 1
    year of age in 6 of 16 German states from 1995 to 2000, and incidence in
    those years ran above the long-term trend (rate ratio 1.26). The paper does
    not say whether ganglioneuroblastoma is counted with neuroblastoma.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:28786082
    reference_title: "Incidence, Survival, and Treatment of Localized and Metastatic Neuroblastoma in Germany 1979-2015."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The population-based median annual age standardized incidence rate (ASR) of neuroblastoma per million children per year in Germany between the periods 1980 and 2015 was 13.2"
    explanation: >-
      The authors' population-based analysis of German Childhood Cancer Registry
      data gives the median of the annual age-standardised incidence rates (Segi
      world standard) for 1980-2015 as 13.2 neuroblastoma cases per million
      children per year, which is 1.32 per 100,000. It is a median of annual
      rates, not a pooled rate for the period, and the paper's Figure 1 gives
      the age band as 0-14 years. The same sentence goes on to give the
      extremes, 8.7 per million in 1981 (incomplete registration) and 17.8 in
      2000 (the last year of the screening trial); the Methods add that case
      numbers before 1986 were not complete enough for epidemiological analysis,
      although the median spans 1980-2015. The paper does not say whether
      ganglioneuroblastoma is counted with neuroblastoma.
  - reference: PMID:28786082
    reference_title: "Incidence, Survival, and Treatment of Localized and Metastatic Neuroblastoma in Germany 1979-2015."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The age-adjusted regression curve (Fig. 1) shows an increase in crude neuroblastoma incidence rates during the period of neuroblastoma screening (RR 1.26; 95% CI 1.17-1.36)"
    explanation: >-
      The authors' age-adjusted trend analysis of German registry incidence in
      children aged 0-14 (trend fitted to 1986-2014 and adjusted for age
      distribution, German reunification and the screening trial) found crude
      incidence during the screening period raised by a rate ratio of 1.26 (95%
      CI 1.17-1.36) relative to the fitted trend. A median taken over 1980-2015
      therefore includes these raised years. The rate ratio is a deviation from
      the fitted trend, not a comparison with a fixed pre-screening baseline,
      and it is a national estimate although screening was offered in only some
      states.
  - reference: PMID:28786082
    reference_title: "Incidence, Survival, and Treatment of Localized and Metastatic Neuroblastoma in Germany 1979-2015."
    supports: SUPPORT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Urine screening for catecholamine metabolites to detect early neuroblastoma was offered to children at approximately 1 year of age in 6 of 16 German States from 1995 to 2000"
    explanation: >-
      Gives the dates and scope of the screening period: urine screening for
      catecholamine metabolites was offered at about 1 year of age in 6 of 16
      German states from 1995 to 2000. This Methods sentence describes a
      programme reported separately (the paper's reference 11) and says nothing
      about incidence; the rate ratio comes from the Results sentence above.

      Orphanet's epidemiology table for ORPHA:635 gives a point-prevalence class
