      infants, not an independent finding. The abstract does not define 'infant'
      or say how many of its 67 mass-screening cases were infants, so the rate
      may not hold for clinically detected infant tumours.
  downstream:
  - target: Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres
    description: >-
      Loss of ATRX/DAXX complex function permits alternative lengthening of
      telomeres. ATRX mutation is associated with loss of nuclear ATRX protein
      and with ALT, and in one series every ALT tumour carried an ATRX or DAXX
      alteration. Without ATRX, histone H3.3 is not efficiently deposited at
      telomeric repeats, replication forks stall there, and the telomeres
      undergo the homologous recombination that leads to ALT.
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    intermediate_mechanisms:
    - "Loss of ATRX/DAXX-dependent deposition of histone H3.3 at telomeric repeats"
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:22416102
      reference_title: "Association of age at diagnosis and genetic mutations in patients with neuroblastoma."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: "ATRX mutations were associated with loss of nuclear ATRX protein, longer telomeres and ALT."
      explanation: >-
        In patients' stage 4 neuroblastomas, all 8 ATRX-mutant tumours with
        tissue had complete or mosaic loss of nuclear ATRX protein and the
        ultrabright telomeric FISH signal that is a hallmark of ALT, while only
        1 of 20 ATRX wild-type tumours had ALT. One wild-type tumour with mosaic
        nuclear ATRX loss had no ALT. Longer telomeres by sequencing did not
        separate the groups significantly (8 of 10 mutant, 12 of 30 wild-type).
        These are co-occurrences, not a causal test, and the paper reports ATRX
        immunostaining, not DAXX protein or complex levels.
    - reference: PMID:25487495
      reference_title: "Clinical features of ATRX or DAXX mutated neuroblastoma."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: "In NBLs, ALT was caused by ATRX or DAXX alterations."
      explanation: >-
        In a separate clinical series of 121 neuroblastomas, 10 of the 11
        tumours with ALT carried ATRX alterations and 1 a DAXX mutation, while
        only 1 of the 110 tumours with normal or shortened telomeres carried
        either. The causal wording is the authors' reading of this co-occurrence
        in 11 ALT cases, and the DAXX evidence is a single tumour. The abstract
        reports gene alterations found by sequencing, not ATRX or DAXX protein
        levels, so reading them as reduced complex abundance is an inference.
    - reference: PMID:32060267
      reference_title: "MYCN amplification and ATRX mutations are incompatible in neuroblastoma."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: BACKGROUND
      evidence_source: IN_VITRO
      snippet: "In cells lacking ATRX, H3.3 is not efficiently deposited at the telomeric G-rich regions, G4 structures form, and replication forks stall ... Consequently, telomeres undergo homologous recombination leading to alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT)"
      explanation: >-
        The introduction of this neuroblastoma study, citing earlier work,
        states the step named as this edge's intermediate: in cells lacking
        ATRX, histone H3.3 is not efficiently deposited at telomeric G-rich
        regions, G4 structures form and replication forks stall, and the
        telomeres then undergo homologous recombination, leading to ALT. Support
        is indirect because this restates cell biology from earlier work rather
        than a measurement in neuroblastoma tumours, and it concerns loss of
        ATRX, not of DAXX. In the paper's own experiments, ATRX knockdown
        changed neither telomere content nor ALT status in any cell line tested
        after two weeks.
- name: Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres
  description: >-
    Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), the recombination-based telomere
    maintenance mechanism that works without telomerase. Its measured frequency
    depends on cohort and assay: C-circle screening classified 9.2% of a
    720-tumour screening cohort as ALT-positive, ALT-associated PML nuclear
    bodies marked 49 of 273 pretreatment neuroblastomas, and the C-circle assay
    marked 25 of 107 high-risk tumours from patients older than 18 months. In a
    registry cohort of 40 relapsed tumours, 47.5% were ALT-positive. ATRX
    alterations are found in only about half to 60% of ALT tumours. In primary
    tumours, ALT and the routes to telomerase activation occur almost mutually
    exclusively, and ATRX mutation and MYCN amplification co-occurred in only 1
    of 819 tumours. ALT-positive neuroblastomas proliferate slowly, with a
    protracted clinical course, yet children with these tumours have a dismal
    outcome. About a third of ALT-positive tumours present with localized
    disease classified as low or intermediate risk, and in one cohort survival
    did not differ between ALT-positive tumours classified high risk and those
    classified low or intermediate risk.
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  biological_processes:
  - preferred_term: telomere maintenance via recombination
    modifier: INCREASED
    term:
      id: GO:0000722
      label: telomere maintenance via recombination
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:32291317
    reference_title: "Telomere Maintenance Mechanisms Define Clinical Outcome in High-Risk Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "ALT was identified in 23.4% of high-risk neuroblastoma tumors and genomic alterations in ATRX were detected in 60% of ALT tumors; 40% of ALT tumors lacked genomic alterations in known ALT-associated genes."
    explanation: >-
      In a Children's Oncology Group cohort of patient primary tumours taken at
      diagnosis, this abstract sentence states the paper's own result:
      C-circle-defined ALT in 23.4% of high-risk tumours, with ATRX alterations
      in 60% of ALT tumours. The other 40% were ATRX wild-type by Sanger
      sequencing, and no DAXX, H3F3A or SMARCAL1 alteration was detected in
      them. The 60% (15 of 25) includes two cases called only from RNA-seq
      overexpression of in-frame-fusion ATRX transcripts; DNA sequencing alone
      found ATRX alterations in 13 of 23 sequenced ALT tumours (57%).
  - reference: PMID:32291317
    reference_title: "Telomere Maintenance Mechanisms Define Clinical Outcome in High-Risk Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Of the 107 high-risk tumors (age > 18 months), 25 (23.4%; 95% CI: 15.3-31.4%) were positive for the ALT biomarker C-circles"
    explanation: >-
      This Results sentence gives the count behind the 23.4%: among 134 primary
      tumours taken at diagnosis and assayed, 25 of the 107 high-risk tumours
      from patients older than 18 months were positive for C-circles, a highly
      specific DNA marker of ALT measured by qPCR. It supports the frequency,
      assay and population, not the share of ALT tumours with ATRX alterations.
      The figure is specific to this assay: three APB-positive tumours fell
      below the C-circle cutoff, and counting either marker gives 28 of 107 ALT
      tumours.
  - reference: PMID:33627664
    reference_title: "Alternative lengthening of telomeres in childhood neuroblastoma from genome to proteome."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "9.2% of the neuroblastomas in a screening cohort of 720 tumors were classified as ALT-positive"
    explanation: >-
      C-circle screening of a cohort of 720 neuroblastomas from German and
      Austrian trials and registries classified 9.2% as ALT-positive. Because
      the cohort was not restricted to high-risk disease, this is the
      broadest-spectrum frequency among the cohorts cited here. It is a trial
      and registry series rather than a population-based sample, and C-circle
      frequencies are not directly comparable with those from ALT-associated PML
      nuclear bodies.
  - reference: PMID:33627664
    reference_title: "Alternative lengthening of telomeres in childhood neuroblastoma from genome to proteome."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Importantly, 47.5% of the INFORM tumors were ALT-activated, indicating a strong enrichment of this molecular subgroup in relapsed cases"
    explanation: >-
      The same C-circle assay applied to 40 relapsed neuroblastomas from the
      INFORM registry found 47.5% ALT-positive, which the authors read as strong
      enrichment of ALT among relapsed cases. The cohort is small and not a
      random sample of relapses: the authors note that registry entry requires
      sufficient general condition and a life expectancy of at least three
      months, which may underrepresent the most aggressive, mostly
      MYCN-amplified or TERT-rearranged tumours.
  - reference: PMID:39635126
    reference_title: "Copy-number dosage regulates telomere maintenance and disease-associated pathways in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Alterations at the ATRX locus are key drivers of ALT but only present in ~50% of ALT tumors."
    explanation: >-
      The abstract of this whole-genome and transcriptome study of 115 primary
      neuroblastomas states that alterations at the ATRX locus are key drivers
      of ALT yet are present in only about half of ALT tumours. The sentence
      frames the study and restates earlier work rather than reporting the
      paper's own measurement; the introduction credits the frequency (ATRX
      mutations in 50-60% of ALT-positive neuroblastomas) to earlier studies.
      The figure counts genomic alterations only; the discussion cites earlier
      work finding reduced ATRX protein in ATRX-wild-type ALT-positive
      neuroblastomas.
  - reference: PMID:39635126
    reference_title: "Copy-number dosage regulates telomere maintenance and disease-associated pathways in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Among ALT tumors 9/20 (45%) harbored ATRX alterations and a single tumor (NBL49) a H3F3A missense mutation (p.A48E)."
    explanation: >-
      In the paper's own cohort of 115 primary neuroblastomas, profiled by
      tumour and matched-normal whole-genome sequencing plus tumour RNA-seq, 9
      of the 20 tumours classified as ALT (45%) carried ATRX alterations. This
      supports only the frequency, not that ATRX alterations drive ALT. The ALT
      group is small, and ALT status was inferred from telomere content in the
      sequencing data, checked against ALT-associated PML nuclear bodies and
      C-circles in subsets of 52 and 36 tumours.
  - reference: PMID:35100718
    reference_title: "Telomerase Is a Prognostic Marker of Poor Outcome and a Therapeutic Target in Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "ALT activation was found in 49 of 273 cases (17.9%). All these alterations occurred almost mutually exclusively and were associated with unfavorable prognostic variables and adverse outcome."
    explanation: >-
      This patient series covered 457 pretreatment neuroblastomas, 273 of them
      assessed for ALT by detecting ALT-associated PML nuclear bodies. The
      authors report that ALT and the three events they count as activated
      telomerase (TERT rearrangement, MYCN amplification, or high TERT
      expression without either) occurred almost mutually exclusively and were
      associated with unfavourable prognostic variables and adverse outcome.
      'Almost' means some overlap the abstract does not count, comparisons
      involving ALT cover only the 273 assessed tumours, and only activated
      telomerase was reported as an independent prognostic marker in
      multivariable analyses.
  - reference: PMID:32060267
    reference_title: "MYCN amplification and ATRX mutations are incompatible in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Here we show that ATRX mutations and MYCN amplification are mutually exclusive across all ages and stages in neuroblastoma."
    explanation: >-
      The authors' abstract summary of their own analysis of patient tumours,
      made by merging the COG, TARGET and PCGP data (819 tumours), states the
      exclusivity directly and extends it across all ages and stages. The
      exclusivity is statistical rather than absolute: one of the 819 tumours
      carried both lesions. For infants the result is uninformative, because
      none of the 213 COG patients diagnosed before 18 months had an ATRX
      mutation.
  - reference: PMID:32060267
    reference_title: "MYCN amplification and ATRX mutations are incompatible in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "In the cohort of 819 tumors, ATRX mutations (n = 64) and MYCN amplification (n = 140) showed statistically significant mutual exclusivity (p = 0.0037, Cochrane-Mantel-Haenszel test) (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Note 1). Only 1 of 819 (0.1%) tumors had both lesions."
    explanation: >-
      The authors' pooled analysis of patient tumours (COG, TARGET and PCGP data
      merged) found significant mutual exclusivity of ATRX mutation and MYCN
      amplification among 819 tumours, with only one tumour carrying both, which
      supports near-complete rather than absolute exclusivity. That tumour was
      MYCN-amplified by FISH at the COG neuroblastoma reference lab but not by
      sequencing read depth, and repeat FISH found regional heterogeneity of
      MYCN amplification. In the COG cohort alone, ATRX mutation frequency did
      not differ significantly by MYCN status, so the significance comes from
      the merged data.
  - reference: PMID:33627664
    reference_title: "Alternative lengthening of telomeres in childhood neuroblastoma from genome to proteome."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "ALT-positive neuroblastomas proliferate slowly, which is reflected by a protracted clinical course of disease."
    explanation: >-
      This abstract sentence, from a study screening 760 primary and relapsed
      neuroblastomas for ALT, states both slow proliferation and a protracted
      clinical course. Slow proliferation rests on proteomics of 34 tumours,
      where proliferation-associated protein pathways were lower than in
      telomerase-activated tumours, and on fewer cycling cells than in
      MYCN-amplified tumours. Survival curves (60 ALT-positive vs 34
      MYCN-amplified tumours) showed significantly longer overall survival time
      but similarly poor event-free survival. Both findings are relative to
      telomerase-activated tumours, and the link between them is the authors'
      interpretation rather than a tested relationship.
  - reference: PMID:33627664
    reference_title: "Alternative lengthening of telomeres in childhood neuroblastoma from genome to proteome."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Nevertheless, children with an ALT-positive neuroblastoma have dismal outcome."
    explanation: >-
      Closing abstract sentence of a retrospective neuroblastoma study, resting
      on the authors' own Kaplan-Meier analysis (60 ALT-positive vs 34
      MYCN-amplified tumours). It states that despite the slow proliferation and
      protracted course reported before it, children with ALT-positive
      neuroblastoma have a dismal outcome. In that analysis event-free survival
      was similarly poor to that with MYCN amplification, but overall survival
      was significantly longer, so 'dismal' means long-term outcome. Limitation:
      the cohort was deliberately enriched for ALT tumours, with survival data
      from German GPOH-trial patients (1991-2018), so it gives no
      population-based estimate.
  - reference: PMID:33627664
    reference_title: "Alternative lengthening of telomeres in childhood neuroblastoma from genome to proteome."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "about one third of the ALT-positive neuroblastomas had localized disease and were stratified at diagnosis as low or intermediate risk using a standard risk classification system"
    explanation: >-
      Although ALT was associated with stage 4, high-risk disease and older age
      at diagnosis, about a third of the ALT-positive tumours in this study had
      localized disease and were classified as low or intermediate risk at
      diagnosis, so ALT is not confined to high-risk disease at presentation.
      None of the 83 stage 4S tumours screened was ALT-positive. The sentence
      reports the authors' own cohort and says nothing about outcome.
  - reference: PMID:33627664
    reference_title: "Alternative lengthening of telomeres in childhood neuroblastoma from genome to proteome."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "No difference in event-free or overall survival was observed between patients with ALT-positive tumors stratified into high-risk and those predicted as low/intermediate risk"
    explanation: >-
      In the sequenced, ALT-enriched cohort, event-free and overall survival did
      not differ between patients with ALT-positive tumours classified high risk
      and those classified low or intermediate risk, which the authors read as
      current risk stratification underestimating the poor prognosis of
      ALT-positive tumours. The comparison is retrospective with small groups,
      so the absence of a difference is weak evidence of equivalent outcome, and
      the cohort was deliberately enriched for ALT.
  downstream:
  - target: Unlimited Replicative Potential
    description: >-
      ALT maintains telomere length without telomerase, giving the tumour cells
      that use it an unlimited replicative capacity. High-risk neuroblastoma
      cell lines with neither ALT nor telomerase activity showed continuous
      telomere shortening, and most lost viability in culture.
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:40638875
      reference_title: "Clinical Significance of TERT Promoter Mutations in Neuroblastoma."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: BACKGROUND
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: "Advances in molecular techniques have highlighted the critical role of telomere maintenance mechanisms that stabilize telomeres for unlimited replicative capacity and immortality in the pathogenesis of high-risk neuroblastoma ... Telomere maintenance is mediated by telomerase-dependent (classical) and independent (alternate) pathways."
      explanation: >-
        The introduction of this neuroblastoma clinical cohort study states that
        telomere maintenance mechanisms, which stabilise telomeres for unlimited
        replicative capacity and immortality, have a critical role in high-risk
        neuroblastoma, and that telomere maintenance is mediated by
        telomerase-dependent and telomerase-independent ('alternate') pathways;
        later in the paragraph the authors name this route the alternate
        lengthening of telomeres (ALT) pathway. Support for ALT is indirect
        because the first quoted sentence covers telomere maintenance mechanisms
        as a class. It is cited background about high-risk disease, not this
        study's finding.
    - reference: PMID:24792489
      reference_title: "Alternative lengthening of telomeres in neuroblastoma cell lines is associated with a lack of MYCN genomic amplification and with p53 pathway aberrations."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: BACKGROUND
      evidence_source: IN_VITRO
      snippet: "Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) is a telomerase-independent telomere length maintenance mechanism that enables the unlimited proliferation of a subset of cancer cells."
      explanation: >-
        The opening sentence of this study of 40 neuroblastoma cell lines
        describes alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) as a
        telomerase-independent telomere length maintenance mechanism that
        enables the unlimited proliferation of a subset of cancer cells. It
        names ALT and unlimited proliferation together, but as general
        background about cancer cells rather than a neuroblastoma result, so
        support for neuroblastoma is indirect. The abstract's next sentence says
        only that some neuroblastoma tumours appear to maintain telomere length
        by activating ALT.
    - reference: PMID:32291317
      reference_title: "Telomere Maintenance Mechanisms Define Clinical Outcome in High-Risk Neuroblastoma."
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: IN_VITRO
      snippet: "high-risk neuroblastoma cell lines that were non-ALT, low TERT expressing, and lacked telomerase activity showed continuous shortening of telomeres with growth in vitro and 2 of 3 TERT-L/non-ALT cell lines spontaneously lost viability after multiple passages in culture"
      explanation: >-
        Three patient-derived high-risk neuroblastoma cell lines that lacked ALT
        as well as telomerase activity shortened their telomeres continuously in
        culture, and 2 of 3 spontaneously lost viability, so losing both
        telomere maintenance mechanisms costs replicative capacity, which
        supports this edge by its converse. Viability held up in the third line,
        which had very high telomere content, so the result shows that a
        maintenance mechanism is required for sustained growth, not that ALT
        alone suffices.
- name: Unlimited Replicative Potential
  description: >-
    The ability of tumour cells to keep dividing indefinitely, which a telomere
    maintenance mechanism (telomerase activation or ALT) provides. Its binding,
    increased cell population proliferation, follows the module node it conforms
    to and means expansion continuing past the limit that telomere shortening
    sets on normal cells, not a faster division rate: ALT-positive
    neuroblastomas proliferate more slowly than telomerase-activated ones.
    Aggressive neuroblastomas show a prolonged evolution during which they
    acquire telomere maintenance mechanisms, whereas tumours with a favourable
    prognosis expand clonally after a short evolution. In pretreatment
    neuroblastomas, patients whose tumours lacked a telomere maintenance
    mechanism had an excellent prognosis and those whose tumours had one did
    substantially worse. Within high-risk disease the picture is less clear: in
    one cohort the telomere maintenance groups differed in overall but not in
    event-free survival, and a subset of high-risk tumours lacks significant
    telomere lengthening activity, with cells derived from them proliferating
    for more than 200 population doublings while their telomeres shortened.
  biological_scale: CELLULAR
  conforms_to: "enabling_replicative_immortality#Replicative Immortality"
  biological_processes:
  - preferred_term: cell population proliferation
    modifier: INCREASED
    term:
      id: GO:0008283
      label: cell population proliferation
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:30523111
    reference_title: "A mechanistic classification of clinical phenotypes in neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "We found that patients whose tumors lacked telomere maintenance mechanisms had an excellent prognosis, whereas the prognosis of patients whose tumors harbored telomere maintenance mechanisms was substantially worse."
    explanation: >-
      In a patient cohort, 208 of 416 sequenced pretreatment neuroblastomas were
      assessed for both telomerase activation (MYCN amplification, TERT
      rearrangement or high TERT expression) and ALT (ALT-associated PML nuclear
      bodies). Patients whose tumours lacked a telomere maintenance mechanism
      had an excellent prognosis, while those whose tumours had one did
      substantially worse. Indirect for this node: an outcome association does
      not measure replicative capacity, and the link rests on telomere
      maintenance being essential for immortal proliferation, a premise the
      paper takes from earlier work.
  - reference: PMID:32291317
    reference_title: "Telomere Maintenance Mechanisms Define Clinical Outcome in High-Risk Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Event-free survival was similar among TERT-high, ALT+, or TERT-low/non-ALT patients. However, overall survival (OS) for TERT-low/non-ALT patients was significantly higher relative to TERT-high or ALT patients (log-rank test; P < 0.01) independent of current clinical and molecular prognostic markers."
    explanation: >-
      In 107 stage 4 high-risk patients diagnosed after 18 months of age,
      grouped by C-circle (ALT) status and TERT mRNA above or below the median,
      event-free survival did not differ significantly across the three groups
      (P = 0.137), while overall survival was significantly higher for
      TERT-low/non-ALT patients. The authors attribute this to more successful
      salvage therapy after an event, and hypothesise that tumours lacking a
      telomere maintenance mechanism keep eroding their telomeres, which
      eventually lets salvage therapy eradicate them. Indirect for this node:
      survival does not measure replicative capacity, and the link rests on that
      telomere-erosion hypothesis. Limitations are a single cohort not uniformly
      treated on current protocols and a median TERT cutoff that may not be
      optimal.
  - reference: PMID:28636942
    reference_title: "Extensive Proliferation of Human Cancer Cells with Ever-Shorter Telomeres."
    supports: REFUTE
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Here, we show that a subset of high-risk neuroblastomas (with ~50% 5-year mortality) lacked significant TLM activity."
    explanation: >-
      Bears against this node as a universal feature of high-risk neuroblastoma,
      though not against it in tumours that maintain their telomeres. In patient
      tumours the authors identify a subset of high-risk neuroblastomas that
      lacked significant telomere lengthening mechanism (TLM) activity, TLM
      being their term for telomerase or alternative lengthening of telomeres.
      Indirect from this sentence alone, because the abstract also raises an
      unrecognised lengthening mechanism or a false-negative assay; the
      continued telomere shortening in cells derived from these tumours argues
      against both. The ~50% 5-year mortality describes the high-risk category
      the subset was drawn from, and the abstract gives neither the subset's
      size nor the assay.
  - reference: PMID:28636942
    reference_title: "Extensive Proliferation of Human Cancer Cells with Ever-Shorter Telomeres."
    supports: REFUTE
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    snippet: "Cancer cells derived from these highly aggressive tumors initially had long telomeres and proliferated for >200 population doublings with ever-shorter telomeres."
    explanation: >-
      Cell lines derived from the high-risk neuroblastomas that lacked
      significant TLM activity grew for more than 200 population doublings while
      their telomeres kept shortening, so their extensive proliferation drew
      down a finite telomere reserve rather than reflecting unlimited
      replicative potential. Continued shortening over that many doublings
      argues against a false-negative assay or an unrecognised maintenance
      mechanism. Indirect because the inference to tumour behaviour is from cell
      culture.
  - reference: PMID:36973454
    reference_title: "Neuroblastoma arises in early fetal development and its evolutionary duration predicts outcome."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Neuroblastomas with favorable prognosis expand clonally after short evolution, whereas aggressive neuroblastomas show prolonged evolution during which they acquire telomere maintenance mechanisms."
    explanation: >-
      The quoted conclusion comes from deep whole-genome sequencing and
      molecular-clock analysis of patient neuroblastomas covering the clinical
      spectrum: aggressive tumours evolve over a prolonged period and acquire
      telomere maintenance mechanisms during it, whereas favourable-prognosis
      tumours expand clonally after a short evolution. An independent cohort (n
      = 86) was assembled to test the outcome prediction from the duration of
      evolution; the telomere maintenance enrichment behind this conclusion was
      computed on both cohorts pooled. Indirect for this node: the sentence is
      about when telomere maintenance is acquired, and the link to replicative
      capacity rests on telomere maintenance being what confers it. The order of
      events is reconstructed from single tumour samples, and the rearrangements
      conferring telomere maintenance cannot themselves be timed from mutation
      densities.
  - reference: PMID:36973454
    reference_title: "Neuroblastoma arises in early fetal development and its evolutionary duration predicts outcome."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "12% of early-MRCA tumors but 81% of late-MRCA tumors gained telomere maintenance - via MYCN amplification, ALT or TERT rearrangement - in the combined discovery and validation cohorts"
    explanation: >-
      Across the pooled discovery and validation cohorts, telomere maintenance
      - by MYCN amplification, ALT or TERT rearrangement - had been gained in
      81% of patient tumours whose most recent common ancestor emerged late,
      after a long evolution, against 12% of those with an early common
      ancestor. This quantifies the enrichment behind the timing conclusion. It
      is prevalence by evolutionary class rather than a timing measurement, and
      the authors state that these small rearrangements cannot be timed from
      mutation densities, so acquisition during the prolonged evolution follows
      by inference.
histopathology:
- name: Schwannian Stroma-Poor Neuroblastic Histology
  diagnostic: true
  finding_term:
    preferred_term: Schwannian stroma-poor neuroblastic tumor
  context: Peripheral neuroblastic tumors classified by the INPC, whose prognostic grouping is designed for pediatric tumors
  description: >-
    The defining histology of this entry under the International Neuroblastoma
    Pathology Classification (INPC), which the International Neuroblastoma
    Pathology Committee proposed in 1999 on the framework of the Shimada
    classification with minor modifications. INPC is an age-linked
    classification that depends on the differentiation grade of the
    neuroblasts, their cellular turnover index and the presence or absence of
    Schwannian stromal development. It places peripheral neuroblastic tumors
    in four categories: neuroblastoma (Schwannian stroma-poor), subtyped as
    undifferentiated, poorly differentiated or differentiating;
    ganglioneuroblastoma, intermixed (Schwannian stroma-rich); ganglioneuroma
    (Schwannian stroma-dominant); and ganglioneuroblastoma, nodular. Only the
    stroma-poor neuroblastoma category belongs to this entry. INPC was designed
    for prognostic distinction among pediatric peripheral neuroblastic tumors
    and is not applicable to adult ones, although there is no clear consensus
    on the age that separates the two groups.
  notes: >-
    Left unbound. OLS searches of NCIT on 2026-10-20 for "stroma-poor" and
    "Schwannian stroma" (up to 15 results each) returned NCIT:C3270
    Neuroblastoma, the Shimada classification terms NCIT:C85414 and
    NCIT:C85415, the composite tumor concepts NCIT:C42059 and NCIT:C42060,
    other neuroblastic tumor concepts, findings for other histologies (among
    them NCIT:C42049, NCIT:C42062, NCIT:C42063, NCIT:C42066, NCIT:C42068 and
    NCIT:C42071) and unrelated tumors and drug regimens, but no finding term
    for stroma-poor histology; searches for "Schwannian stroma absent" and
    "limited Schwannian stroma" returned no results. NCIT:C3270, whose
    definition includes the absence of a prominent Schwannian stroma, is this
    entry's own disease concept, and a bound histopathology term is exported
    as a has_phenotype edge from the disease.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:10421272
    reference_title: "Terminology and morphologic criteria of neuroblastic tumors: recommendations by the International Neuroblastoma Pathology Committee."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Based on morphologic criteria defined in this article, NTs were classified into four categories and their subtypes: 1) neuroblastoma (Schwannian stroma-poor), undifferentiated, poorly differentiated, and differentiating; 2) ganglioneuroblastoma, intermixed (Schwannian stroma-rich); 3) ganglioneuroma (Schwannian stroma-dominant), maturing and mature; and 4) ganglioneuroblastoma, nodular"
    explanation: >-
      The 1999 terminology paper of the International Neuroblastoma Pathology
      Committee, whose six member pathologists defined the morphologic criteria
      from a review of 227 cases. It classifies neuroblastic tumors into four
      categories, with neuroblastoma (Schwannian stroma-poor) and its
      undifferentiated, poorly differentiated and differentiating subtypes as
      the first; the quote ends before the stromal label of the fourth. The
      abstract names the neuroblastoma subtypes but gives no criteria for them,
      so this item supports the category scheme, not the subtype definitions.
      In this abstract INPC abbreviates the Committee; the Classification
      itself is reported in a companion article in the same issue
      (PMID:10421273).
  - reference: PMID:10421272
    reference_title: "Terminology and morphologic criteria of neuroblastic tumors: recommendations by the International Neuroblastoma Pathology Committee."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "It is an age-linked classification dependent on the differentiation grade of the neuroblasts, their cellular turnover index, and the presence or absence of Schwannian stromal development."
    explanation: >-
      In the results of its abstract, the International Neuroblastoma
      Pathology Committee describes the prognostic system it adopted, which
      the preceding sentence says is modeled on the one proposed by Shimada
      et al., as an age-linked classification dependent on the differentiation
      grade of the neuroblasts, their cellular turnover index, and the
      presence or absence of Schwannian stromal development. The abstract's
      conclusion names the Committee's proposal the International
      Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification. The abstract gives no survival
      figures, and the quote does not say how the cellular turnover index is
      measured.
  - reference: PMID:10421273
    reference_title: "The International Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification (the Shimada system)."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "The International Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification, a system based on a framework of the Shimada classification with minor modifications, is proposed for international use in assessing NTs."
    explanation: >-
      In its conclusion, the 1999 paper that proposed the classification
      describes it as a system based on a framework of the Shimada
      classification with minor modifications. This supports describing INPC
      as built on the Shimada framework but not identical to it. The authors
      call the changes minor, the paper's own title calls INPC "the Shimada
      system", and the abstract does not say which modifications were made.
      The classification was evaluated on 227 reviewed cases with survival
      analysis.
  - reference: PMID:41612478
    reference_title: "Pathology of peripheral neuroblastic tumors."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: 'It should be noted that since INPC is designed for prognostic distinction among "pediatric" pNTs, it is not applicable to "adult" pNTs even though no clear consensus for separating these two age groups.'
    explanation: >-
      The review states that, since INPC was designed for prognostic
      distinction among pediatric peripheral neuroblastic tumors, it is not
      applicable to adult ones. The same paragraph says adult tumors are still
      histologically diagnosed in the same categories, so the stated limit
      concerns INPC's prognostic grouping, not the diagnosis of these tumors.
      The authors add that there is no clear consensus on the age that
      separates pediatric from adult tumors, so the source does not say where
      the boundary falls. The sentence is the review authors' own statement of
      the classification's scope, with no data or citation attached, so it is
      graded OTHER as an expert statement rather than a study of INPC in
      adults.
- name: Undifferentiated Neuroblastoma Subtype
  finding_term:
    preferred_term: undifferentiated neuroblastoma (INPC subtype)
    term:
      id: NCIT:C42046
      label: Undifferentiated Neuroblastoma
  frequency: VERY_RARE
  context: Diagnostic tumor tissue obtained before chemotherapy or irradiation
  description: >-
    INPC subtype of the neuroblastoma category composed of tumor cells without
    clearly recognizable neurite production. Accordingly, in routine practice
    the diagnosis is confirmed by immunohistochemistry, in which positive
    nuclear staining for PHOX2B is critical. INPC classifies every
    neuroblastoma of the undifferentiated subtype as unfavorable histology,
    regardless of the patient's age. It is the rarest subtype: 177 of 4,680
    Schwannian stroma-poor tumors (3.8%) classified at central review in the
    Children's Oncology Group Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory
    between August 2001 and March 2012, on specimens obtained before
    chemotherapy or irradiation.
  notes: >-
    NCIT:C42046 defines this subtype by the absence of differentiating
    neuroblasts, a criterion a poorly differentiated tumor can also meet
    (NCIT:C42047 defines that subtype by differentiating neuroblasts making up
    less than five percent of the tumor cells). INPC separates the two
    subtypes by neurite production, and the description follows the INPC
    wording.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:41612478
    reference_title: "Pathology of peripheral neuroblastic tumors."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Undifferentiated subtype: Tumors in this subtype are composed of cells without clearly recognizable neurite production (Fig. 1B). Accordingly, positive nuclear immunostaining for PHOX2B is critical for confirming the diagnosis in routine practice. The tumor cells seem to have little to no potential for neuroblastic differentiation, and the cases are always classified into the UH group regardless of age of the patients."
    explanation: >-
      In its account of the INPC, the review defines the undifferentiated
      subtype as tumors composed of cells without clearly recognizable neurite
      production, states that positive nuclear PHOX2B immunostaining is
      critical for confirming the diagnosis in routine practice, and states
      that these cases are always classified into the unfavorable histology
      (UH) group regardless of the patient's age. The passage restates the
      classification and a practice recommendation; it reports no new case
      series.
  - reference: PMID:25207821
    reference_title: "Age-dependent prognostic effect by Mitosis-Karyorrhexis Index in neuroblastoma: a report from the Children's Oncology Group."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "A total of 5,929 cases of pNTs were reviewed at the COG Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory, Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, Children's Hospital Los Angeles, Los Angeles, California, between August 1, 2001, and March 31, 2012, and 4680 of them were classified as neuroblastoma (Schwannian stroma-poor) tumors including undifferentiated subtype (177 cases), poorly differentiated subtype (4081 cases), and differentiated subtype (422 cases) based on the review of pathology specimens obtained before starting chemotherapy/irradiation therapy."
    explanation: >-
      Of 4,680 Schwannian stroma-poor neuroblastomas classified at central
      review in the COG Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory
      (Children's Hospital Los Angeles, August 2001 to March 2012), on
      pathology specimens obtained before chemotherapy or irradiation, 177
      were the undifferentiated subtype: 177/4,680 = 3.8%, within the
      VERY_RARE band (under 5%). This is a single reference-laboratory
      central-review series, not a population-based sample.
- name: Poorly Differentiated Neuroblastoma Subtype
  finding_term:
    preferred_term: poorly differentiated neuroblastoma (INPC subtype)
    term:
      id: NCIT:C42047
      label: Poorly Differentiated Neuroblastoma
  frequency: VERY_FREQUENT
  context: Diagnostic tumor tissue obtained before chemotherapy or irradiation
  description: >-
    INPC subtype in which the tumor cells produce neurites, with or without
    Homer Wright rosette formation, detectable on H&E staining; neuropil is
    present, but fewer than 5% of tumor cells show ganglionic differentiation.
    By differentiation grade, INPC places it in favorable histology when the
    patient is diagnosed younger than 18 months (up to 547 days) and in
    unfavorable histology from 18 months (548 days); a favorable assignment
    also requires a low or intermediate mitosis-karyorrhexis index (see INPC
    Favorable Histology). It is the commonest subtype: 4,081 of 4,680
    Schwannian stroma-poor tumors (87.2%) classified at central review in the
    Children's Oncology Group Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference Laboratory
    between August 2001 and March 2012.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:41612478
    reference_title: "Pathology of peripheral neuroblastic tumors."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Poorly differentiated subtype: Tumor cells in this subtype are characterized by their neurite production, with or without Homer Wright rosette formation, detectable by H&E staining (Fig. 1C)."
    explanation: >-
      In its account of the INPC, the review characterizes the poorly
      differentiated subtype by tumor-cell neurite production, with or without
      Homer Wright rosette formation, detectable by H&E staining. The review
      restates the INPC criteria rather than reporting a cohort, and this
      passage gives no percentage threshold for differentiating neuroblasts.
  - reference: PMID:41294259
    reference_title: "Histologic Response to Induction Chemotherapy in High-Risk Neuroblastoma."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Tumor differentiation was scored based on the proportion of differentiating neuroblasts and presence of neuropil as undifferentiated (no signs of maturation, no differentiated neuroblasts, or neuropil), poorly differentiated (neuropil present but < 5% ganglionic differentiation), or differentiating (> 5% ganglionic differentiation)"
    explanation: >-
      The methods of a study of paired diagnostic and resection specimens
      from 94 patients with high-risk neuroblastoma enrolled in Children's
      Oncology Group trials give the INPC differentiation grades the authors
      scored, following the INPC publications they cite: poorly differentiated
      tumors have neuropil but under 5% ganglionic differentiation, scored as
      the proportion of differentiating neuroblasts, and differentiating
      tumors have over 5%. The sentence restates the INPC criteria; the study
      applies the threshold and does not derive it.
  - reference: PMID:41612478
    reference_title: "Pathology of peripheral neuroblastic tumors."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "When the patient with a tumor in this subtype is diagnosed less than 18 months (547 days) of age, the case is classified into the FH group. While the patient with tumor having the same histology of NB, poorly differentiated subtype but diagnosed over 18 months (548 days) of age is considered to have no potential of neuroblastic differentiation and tumor maturation, and the case is classified into UH group."
    explanation: >-
      The review states the INPC age rule for the poorly differentiated
      subtype: a case diagnosed at less than 18 months (547 days) is classified
      into the favorable histology (FH) group, and one diagnosed over 18 months
      (548 days) into the unfavorable histology (UH) group. Elsewhere the
      review pairs 548 days with 18 months or more, so 547 days is the last
      day under 18 months. This passage gives the grade criterion only; the
      review's separate MKI paragraph adds that high-MKI tumors indicate a poor
      prognosis at any age, so a poorly differentiated tumor diagnosed under 18
      months is favorable histology only with a low or intermediate MKI.
  - reference: PMID:25207821

- name: Differentiating Neuroblastoma Subtype
  finding_term:
    preferred_term: differentiating neuroblastoma (INPC subtype)
    term:
      id: NCIT:C42048
      label: Differentiating Neuroblastoma
  frequency: OCCASIONAL
  context: Diagnostic tumor tissue obtained before chemotherapy or irradiation
  description: >-
    INPC subtype in which more than 5% of tumor cells have the appearance of
    differentiating neuroblasts, defined by synchronous nuclear and
    cytoplasmic differentiation: cytoplasmic and nuclear enlargement, a
    cytoplasmic diameter at least twice the nuclear diameter, and an
    eccentrically located nucleus with vesicular chromatin and a single
    prominent nucleolus. By differentiation grade, INPC places it in favorable
    histology when the patient is diagnosed younger than 5 years (up to 1824
    days), provided the mitosis-karyorrhexis index also qualifies (see INPC
    Favorable Histology); from 5 years (1825 days) a favorable assignment
    requires further maturation beyond the neuroblastoma category. 422 of
    4,680 Schwannian stroma-poor tumors (9.0%) classified at central review
    in the Children's Oncology Group Neuroblastoma Pathology Reference
    Laboratory between August 2001 and March 2012 were of this subtype.
  notes: >-
    PMID:25207821 and the abstract of PMID:10421273 call this subtype
    "differentiated"; the INPC name, used in PMID:10421272 and PMID:41612478,
    is "differentiating".

    reference_title: "Pathology of peripheral neuroblastic tumors."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS

    snippet: "More than 5% of tumor cells should have an appearance of differentiating neuroblasts (Fig. 1D). By definition, those differentiating neuroblasts demonstrate synchronous differentiation of the nucleus and cytoplasm: They are characterized by cytoplasmic and nuclear enlargement, cytoplasmic diameter measuring at least twice the nuclear diameter, and eccentrically located nucleus with a vesicular chromatin pattern and a single prominent nucleolus."
    explanation: >-
      From the review's paragraph on the differentiating subtype of the INPC
      neuroblastoma category: more than 5% of tumor cells should have the
      appearance of differentiating neuroblasts, which by definition show
      synchronous differentiation of nucleus and cytoplasm, with cytoplasmic
      and nuclear enlargement, a cytoplasmic diameter at least twice the
      nuclear diameter, and an eccentrically located nucleus with a vesicular
      chromatin pattern and a single prominent nucleolus. It is a consensus
      diagnostic definition restated in a review, with no patient data, so it
      is graded OTHER.
  - reference: PMID:41612478
    reference_title: "Pathology of peripheral neuroblastic tumors."
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "Tumors in this subtype are classified into the FH Group in patients diagnosed less than 5 years (1824 days) of age. To be qualified as having FH pNTs, patients over 5 years (1825 days) of age should have further tumor maturation towards GNB-i or GN (see below)."
    explanation: >-
      The quoted sentences close the review's paragraph on the differentiating
      subtype, so "this subtype" is the differentiating subtype. They classify
      these tumors as favorable histology (FH) when the patient is diagnosed
      under 5 years of age (up to 1824 days); from 5 years (1825 days), FH
      requires further maturation beyond the neuroblastoma category. The rule
      is given by grade alone: in its next paragraph the review adds the
      age-linked mitosis-karyorrhexis index (MKI) criterion and notes that
      even differentiating neuroblastomas with low MKI diagnosed over 5 years
      are classified as unfavorable histology.
